- Oregon's first-in-the-nation experiment with decriminalizing drugs will expire on Sunday as a new law (HB4002) takes effect, making possession of small amounts of hard drugs a crime again.
- The new law gives those caught with illicit drugs (fentanyl, heroin, meth) a choice: either be charged with possession or undergo treatment (behavioral health program + "deflection program") to avoid fines.
- Personal-use possession would be a misdemeanor punishable by up to six months in jail.
- Aims to make it easier for police to crack down on drug use in public and introduces harsher penalties for selling drugs near places like parks.
- The law encourages, but does not mandate, counties to create treatment alternatives to divert people from criminal justice system toward addiction and mental health services.
- Backers say this allows counties to develop programs based on resources; opponents say it may create confusing and inequitable patchwork.
- Quote from Portland police chief Bob Day: "The criteria is very narrow to meet deflection: no other charges, no warrants, no violent behavior, medically stable."
- If a person meets deflection requirements, officers will call the county’s deflection dispatch line to provide basic info, determine eligibility, and connect them to a mobile behavioral health outreach team that will have 30 minutes to make contact.
- Day: "If the behavioral health people cannot be there within 30 minutes, we’re going to go to jail. We’re not able to just wait around."
